articles.title: NATO Ties to Donbas Withdrawal Floated in US-Russia Talks
articles.desc: US negotiators raised linking NATO membership to a Ukrainian withdrawal from Donbas; Zelenskiy said he would put any territorial concession to a national referendum.
articles.h1: NATO Ties to Donbas Withdrawal Floated in US-Russia Talks
articles.deck: US negotiators raised linking NATO membership to a Ukrainian withdrawal from Donbas; Zelenskiy said he would put any territorial concession to a national referendum.
articles.body:
A Bargain Raised Behind Closed Doors

KYIV, Nov 14 - US negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine's potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi. This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskiy said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'" he said. "That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation." Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia's full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskiy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum. Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, he dismissed Russia's call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics of ending the war are agreed.

What Was Said and What Was Not

"We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first," he said. US President Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said on Saturday that the two sides had set out "maximalist positions" in the talks this week, but in private discussions both "understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war." Kushner added that "serious and constructive work continues among those of us committed to finding solutions."

The territorial question is not new to the table, but attaching it to NATO membership is. For Kyiv, a withdrawal from Donbas would cross a line written into its constitution and repeated in public statements since 2022; for Moscow, NATO expansion to include Ukraine has been the stated casus belli. A US-mediated swap of land for an alliance card therefore touches both sides' founding positions at once, which is why Zelenskiy reached for the referendum device rather than a direct yes or no.

A Referendum Route with Many Moving Parts

Whether it becomes consequential depends on three drivers. First, whether Washington is prepared to extend an Article 5-style guarantee to territory it would be defending, since a NATO pledge is only as credible as the forces behind it. Second, whether European capitals, now Ukraine's largest financial and military backers, will underwrite the reconstruction bill that a deal of this size implies.

Third, whether the Ukrainian public can be brought to ratify a loss of land, a step no government in Kyiv has yet accepted in advance. A proposal floated in a closed room is not a commitment, and both capitals have walked away from comparably shaped ideas before.

There is a plausible path in which none of this holds. A referendum can be deferred indefinitely, a security package can be watered down to equipment pledges, and the linkage can be dropped quietly in the next round if either side balks. Talks in Abu Dhabi already ended without a major breakthrough, and a prisoner exchange involving more than 1,000 people is the only concrete output so far.

The Most Likely Next Step

The most probable outcome is that the linkage survives as a negotiating position rather than a signed term, and that the next round of trilateral talks opens with a working document that pairs a ceasefire sequence with a security-guarantee schedule, leaving the territorial question to a later stage.

That scenario holds only if the United States keeps the proposal on the table and if Kyiv can show its public a guarantee package substantial enough to make a referendum conceivable; without those two conditions, the idea is likely to be filed alongside earlier frameworks that were raised and then shelved.

articles.title: Brazil Election: Bolsonaro Refuses to Concede to Lula
articles.desc: Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede Brazil election to Lula, raising protest risks and market turmoil. Analysis of international and economic fallout.
articles.h1: Brazil Election: Bolsonaro Refuses to Concede to Lula
articles.deck: Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede Brazil election to Lula, raising protest risks and market turmoil. Analysis of international and economic fallout.
articles.body:
Brazil's disputed presidential election

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won a historic fourth term in Sunday's presidential runoff. The senator, son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, is challenging the result and asking for it to be annulled.

The dispute centers on a late-Sunday decision by a Supreme Court justice appointed by Lula. That justice extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities. Flavio Bolsonaro called the extension improper and said recognizing the result was impossible.

His petition faces steep odds. Bolsonaro trails Lula by more than four million votes, a margin analysts say makes annulment unlikely. His own campaign had sought a voting extension because of heavy rains in the conservative-leaning south, which weakens his argument.

Even so, the refusal to concede carries risk. Observers warn it could spark protests in a country where faith in the electoral system and judicial independence has been strained in recent years.

Jair Bolsonaro plunged Brazil into a deep democratic crisis after the 2022 election, when supporters stormed government buildings. He later received a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup.

Lula's win defied polls, precedent, and global anti-incumbent sentiment. He trailed in the first round but convinced voters to return for the runoff. During the campaign he highlighted cuts to poverty and inequality, plus record low unemployment, illiteracy, and deforestation.

International reaction and diplomatic stakes

While Bolsonaro contested the result at home, foreign leaders moved quickly to recognize Lula's victory. Congratulations came from the European Union, Mexico, France, Canada, India, and Russia.

French President Emmanuel Macron said France and Brazil had much to build together. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said democracy and multilateralism had won in Brazil.

The Kremlin welcomed Lula's re-election and praised his contribution to bilateral ties and to BRICS. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy congratulated Lula on remarkable results and looked forward to expanded cooperation.

Notable absences included the White House, the US State Department, and Argentine President Javier Milei, none of which immediately commented.

The result is set to disappoint the administration of US President Donald Trump. Trump's State Department had led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power. This silence contrasts with the rapid recognition offered by most other governments and signals a complex diplomatic landscape for Lula's fourth term.

Market and fiscal implications

Investors reacted nervously to the outcome. Brazilian assets fell sharply as markets reassessed the country's fiscal outlook under Lula.

November futures for the Brazilian real dropped more than ten percent. The iShares MSCI Brazil exchange-traded fund fell twenty-six percent in premarket trading. Some long-dated Brazilian sovereign bonds lost more than two cents on the dollar.

Pantheon Macroeconomics chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia said the initial sell-off could moderate as election-related positions are unwound. He added that investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure.

Lula also faces a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of right-wing voting recast the legislature against him.

Political scientist Carlos Melo of Insper in Sao Paulo said the challenges are countless. Lula took a conciliatory tone after the win, saying no one must like the elected president but he was put in place to govern for everyone. His fourth term will test whether that conciliation can deliver both fiscal credibility and governability.

articles.title: Understanding currency depreciation: a mechanics explainer
articles.desc: A falling currency is a number, not a mechanism. Three distinct channels produce it, and the same move means opposite things depending on which one is running.
articles.h1: Understanding currency depreciation: a mechanics explainer
articles.deck: A falling currency is a number, not a mechanism. Three distinct channels produce it, and the same move means opposite things depending on which one is running.
articles.body:
“The currency fell” is a statement about a number. It is not a mechanism, and on its own it tells you almost nothing about what happens next. Economists identify at least three distinct channels, and they frequently point in opposite directions.

Channel one: the balance of payments

If a country imports more than it earns, the shortfall must be financed. Either foreign investors supply the currency (capital account surplus) or the currency is sold to buy the difference. Persistent financing needs mean persistent selling, which depreciates the currency and, in turn, raises the price of imports.

Under this channel the exchange rate is doing its job: it is adjusting to a real imbalance. The depreciation is a symptom, not a crisis.

Channel two: the interest-rate differential

A currency with a materially higher policy rate attracts carry trades, which supports it. When that support disappears because rates converge or because a risk-premium shock makes investors unwilling to hold the currency at all, the exchange rate can fall quickly and by a lot — the carry unwinds on the way down, not just on the way up.

Under this channel the depreciation is a symptom of a change in the willingness to hold the asset, which is why it is often discontinuous.

Channel three: the risk premium

Some currencies carry an implicit discount for political or institutional risk. That discount widens when uncertainty rises, independently of trade balances or rates entirely. This channel has no relationship to the current account at all, which is why a country running a large surplus can still see a severe depreciation.

Why the same fall means opposite things

Two depreciations, two different meanings
FeatureOrderly adjustmentRisk-premium shock
Current accountDeficitSurplus or balanced
Rate differentialUnchangedUnchanged or wider
SpeedGradualDiscontinuous
Credit spreadsStableWiden together
Implication for inflationImport prices rise modestlyPass-through plus risk of second-round effects

The diagnostic that separates them is whether credit spreads and sovereign yields move in the same direction as the currency. If they do, you are looking at a risk premium. If the currency falls while spreads stay calm, you are more likely looking at a balance-of-payments adjustment.

What this means in practice

“Depreciation is good for growth” is a summary of one channel and nothing else. A competitiveness-led adjustment can raise net exports. A risk-premium-driven fall raises the domestic cost of importing fuel and food while the currency that buys those imports weakens, and it does so at the same time as foreign-currency debt becomes more expensive to service.

Identify the channel before deciding what the move means. The number is the same in all three cases.

articles.title: What a central bank balance sheet tells you that the rate does not
articles.desc: The judgement calls on top of the mechanics — and the three situations where the framework should be abandoned rather than used.
articles.h1: What a central bank balance sheet tells you that the rate does not
articles.deck: The judgement calls on top of the mechanics — and the three situations where the framework should be abandoned rather than used.
articles.body:
This is a companion to our research note on reading central bank balance sheets. The note sets out the mechanics. This one is about the judgement calls that sit on top of them — the places where an analyst can talk themselves into a position the data does not support.

The asymmetry that flatters the signal

An expanding balance sheet is a commitment. A contracting one is often an accounting artefact of maturities. When reinvestment ends, the portfolio shrinks mechanically until someone actively sells, which almost nobody does. So “the balance sheet contracted” is weak evidence of tightening intent, while “it expanded” is strong evidence of easing intent.

Any framework that weights the two signals equally will over-read tightening and under-read easing. That is a modelling choice, and it is usually made silently.

Composition beats size, every time

Consider two central banks with portfolios of identical size. One holds short-dated bills. The other holds long-dated bonds acquired years ago and is simply letting them run off. Their published balance sheets have the same headline number and opposite policy content.

This is the single most common analytical error we see in commentary on quantitative policy: quoting a total and reading intent into it. The composition tells you what was decided; the total only tells you what has happened to happen.

When the framework is the wrong tool

Three situations defeat it, and in all three the honest response is to say so rather than to produce a number.

  • Funding stress. Expansion as market plumbing. Intent is absent from the signal entirely.
  • Fiscal dominance. When a central bank is absorbing a domestic debt issuance that keeps rates from rising, portfolio growth reflects the fiscal position, not an independent monetary choice.
  • Small open economies. Foreign holdings of domestic currency contaminate the liability side and, through it, the reading of intent.

The practical discipline

State the episode count behind any timing estimate. Ours rests on a handful of post-2008 cases; that is a prior, not a finding, and it would be dishonest to quote it without that caveat attached.

Then name the observation that would change your mind. If you cannot say what would falsify the read, you are not analysing — you are narrating.

articles.title: The balance sheet is the policy: reading central banks
articles.desc: Markets price the rate decision, then react to what the central bank did to its portfolio. The gap between those two events is where the mispricing sits.
articles.h1: The balance sheet is the policy: reading central banks
articles.deck: Markets price the rate decision, then react to what the central bank did to its portfolio. The gap between those two events is where the mispricing sits.
articles.body:
When a central bank changes its policy rate, the statement, the projections and the press conference absorb nearly all of the attention. That is reasonable: the rate is the cleanest and fastest-moving expression of policy. It is not the only expression, and for most major central banks it is no longer the dominant one.

On the liability side of a balance sheet sit reserves and, increasingly, interest-bearing deposits — obligations the bank owes the banking system and the public. Those follow the policy rate mechanically. On the asset side sit securities bought outright: government bonds, agency debt, and in some cases corporate paper and exchange-traded funds. That side is where intention lives, because it changes only when a committee decides to change it.

Why the asset side leads

Asset purchases and sales are slow, large and deliberate. A rate cut can be reversed at the next scheduled meeting; a balance sheet that has grown by fifteen per cent of GDP is not unwound by a single decision. That inertia is what makes the asset side informative. It reveals where a committee has concluded it wants to be, expressed in a form that survives changes of mind about the near-term path of rates.

The practical implication is a timing lead. Our reading of the post-2008 and post-2020 policy sequences is that meaningful changes in the asset side preceded comparable changes in the stance of the policy rate by somewhere between two and three quarters. That is a rough estimate drawn from a small number of episodes, not a measured constant, and it should be treated as a prior to test rather than a rule to apply.

What to read, and in what order

Three series carry most of the signal, and all three are published by the central bank itself or by a national statistical agency — not by a bank’s commentary.

  • Holding-period composition. The share of the portfolio in bills versus longer-dated coupons. A rising bill share signals a flatter, more defensive posture; a falling share signals duration being taken on. This series moves first and moves most clearly.
  • Reinvestment and runoff rates. The monthly caps on what is allowed to mature without replacement. These are published in advance, which makes them the one part of the asset side that is genuinely forecastable rather than inferred after the fact.
  • Total size relative to trend inflation. The crudest measure, and the one most often quoted without context. Only interpretable alongside the first two.

Read them in that order. Composition leads, the published runoff caps confirm, and the headline size is a summary rather than a signal.

Where this framework fails

It fails in a specific and predictable way: during a funding crisis, when a central bank expands its balance sheet to absorb a shock in a market it does not control. That expansion carries no information about intended policy. Any framework that reads size as intent will misread that episode badly. Separating a policy action from a plumbing action is the hardest part of the work and the part most worth getting wrong carefully.

It also degrades in small open economies, where the domestic central bank’s balance sheet is heavily influenced by foreign holdings of domestic currency. The asset side stops being a clean read on domestic intent.

What the framework implies

For asset allocation the useful output is not a forecast of the next rate decision. It is a prior on the shape of the policy path: how much duration a committee is willing to add, how quickly, and what would cause it to reverse. Where the asset side has been expanding while the market prices a shallow path, that gap is where the return is. Where the asset side is contracting while the market prices aggressive easing, it is where the loss is.

Neither gap is a certainty. They are observations about where to look harder.
